title: Training-of-Trainers (ToT): Teach Adults and Build Trainers
subtitle: Design, deliver and evaluate practical trainings for women in your community, and prepare other women to train well too.
description: Learn how adults learn, how to design a training with ADDIE and SMART objectives, how to facilitate with participatory methods, and how to evaluate results with Kirkpatrick's four levels. You will finish with a tested training package, a ToT portfolio and a 90-day plan to cascade your training safely and with quality.
outcomes: Apply Knowles' adult learning principles and Kolb's experiential learning cycle to design engaging sessions
Run a needs analysis and write SMART learning objectives with Bloom's verbs
Build a timed session plan and facilitate it with participatory techniques
Run microteaching and give structured feedback to new trainers
Evaluate training at Kirkpatrick Levels 1 to 3 and write an honest one-page report
Assemble a training package, cost it, and plan a quality-controlled cascade
audience: Women leaders, community mobilisers, cooperative and faith group coordinators, and experienced practitioners who want to teach what they know and prepare others to train.
tools: A phone with a camera and WhatsApp (for notes, timers and follow-up)
Flip chart paper, markers, masking tape and sticky notes (or cut paper)
Access to a small group of 5 to 20 people for practice sessions
Printed or handwritten consent and attendance forms

modules.title: Foundations: How Adults Learn and How a ToT Works
modules.overview: Before you can train other trainers, you need a clear picture of what a Training-of-Trainers is, why cascades succeed or fail, and how adults actually learn. This module covers the cascade model, Knowles' principles of adult learning, Kolb's experiential learning cycle, and how to prepare a safe, inclusive training space.

lessons.title: What a Training-of-Trainers is and how the cascade works
objectives: Explain the difference between a training and a Training-of-Trainers
Describe how a cascade model multiplies reach, step by step
Identify the main reason cascades lose quality and two ways to prevent it
Name the roles in a ToT team: master trainer, trainer, co-facilitator and participant

blocks.text: A normal training teaches people a skill they will use themselves: bookkeeping, hand washing, savings group rules, safe food handling. A **Training-of-Trainers (ToT)** teaches people two things at once: the skill itself, and **how to teach that skill to others**. Graduates of a ToT go back to their communities, churches, cooperatives or women's groups and run the same training there.

blocks.name: teaching
blocks.alt: A woman teaching a small group in front of a board
blocks.caption: In a ToT you learn the content and also practise teaching it, so you can lead your own group afterwards.

blocks.text: This is why NGOs, government agencies, faith groups and networks like WODDI use ToTs. One small team of experienced trainers cannot reach every village or market. But if they train 20 people properly, and each of those 20 trains 25 more, the message reaches 500 people. This chain is called a **cascade**.
Who does what in a ToT

head: Role
What she does
Example
rows: Designs the programme, trains the trainers, checks quality later
A WODDI programme lead who wrote the savings group curriculum
Runs the training for her own community using the trainer guide
A women's leader in a church or market association
Shares the session, watches time, supports group work, gives feedback
A second trainer who leads energisers and records attendance
Learns the skill and uses it in daily life
A trader who learns to keep a daily sales book

blocks.text: Why cascades lose quality

Every time knowledge passes from one level to the next, some of it can be lost, changed or simplified. Trainers and researchers call this **dilution** or the "watering down" effect. Think of the game where one person whispers a sentence to the next person in a line. By the tenth person, the sentence has changed. A cascade without good materials and follow-up can behave the same way.

Dilution happens for predictable reasons: the ToT was too short for trainers to practise, there was no written trainer guide, trainers were chosen because of status rather than skill, or nobody checked the first trainings at the next level. The good news is that each cause has a fix.

items: **A written trainer guide** with the exact key messages, activities and timings, so every trainer teaches the same core content.
**Practice inside the ToT**: every trainer teaches at least one real session and receives feedback before she leaves.
**Selection by criteria**: choose trainers who know the topic, communicate well and have time to train, not only those with titles.
**Follow-up support**: a master trainer observes or calls in on early sessions and answers questions on a WhatsApp group.
**Simple evaluation tools**: the same short test and feedback form used at every level, so you can see where quality drops.

blocks.title: A simple three-level cascade
items: Master trainers design
ToT trains 20 trainers
Trainers run local sessions
Participants apply skill
Follow-up checks quality
blocks.caption: Each step multiplies reach, and the last step catches dilution before it spreads.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning the reach of a cascade
blocks.context: For example, Amaka coordinates a women's network in Anambra. She wants to teach basic record keeping to market women in six local government areas within three months.
steps: She selects 18 trainers, three per local government area, using criteria: can read and write, keeps her own business records, and is trusted in her market.
She plans a three-day ToT, with day three given almost entirely to practice teaching and feedback.
Each trainer agrees to run two sessions of about 15 women each within six weeks. Reach: 18 trainers x 2 sessions x 15 women = 540 women.
She builds in quality checks: she will personally observe one session in each local government area (six visits) and every trainer sends attendance lists and test scores to a WhatsApp group.
She plans for drop-out honestly: if only 15 of the 18 trainers complete both sessions, reach is 15 x 2 x 15 = 450 women.
blocks.result: Amaka sets a realistic target of 450 to 540 women and protects quality with practice, a trainer guide, observation and shared evaluation forms.

blocks.title: Smaller and stronger beats bigger and weaker
blocks.text: A ToT of 15 to 25 participants usually allows everyone to practise teaching and receive feedback. With 50 participants, most people only watch. If funders push for larger numbers, run two smaller ToTs instead of one big one.

blocks.title: A ToT is not a lecture about training
blocks.text: Participants in a ToT should spend much of their time doing what they will later do: practising sessions, giving feedback, running activities and using evaluation forms. If your ToT agenda is mostly presentations, rebalance it so that at least a third of the time is practice teaching.

By the end of this course you will design a short training, run a practice session, collect feedback and evaluation data, and put together a portfolio that shows you can train others and support them to train well too.

takeaways: A ToT teaches both the content and how to teach it
A cascade multiplies reach: trainers x sessions x participants per session
Dilution is the main risk; written guides, practice and follow-up reduce it
Choose trainers by clear criteria, not status alone

activity.title: Sketch your own cascade
steps: Choose one skill you know well and could teach (for example, savings group record keeping or kitchen hygiene).
Decide how many trainers you could train in one ToT and how many sessions each could run.
Calculate expected reach, and a second figure assuming some trainers drop out.
List three quality checks you will use to prevent dilution.
activity.evidence: A one-page note or photo of your cascade sketch with your reach calculation and three quality checks.

lessons.title: How adults learn: Knowles' principles and Kolb's cycle
objectives: List the six assumptions of adult learning described by Malcolm Knowles
Describe the four stages of Kolb's experiential learning cycle
Design a short activity that takes learners through all four stages
Explain why lecture alone is weak for adult learners

blocks.text: Adults are not big children sitting in a classroom. They come with years of experience, responsibilities at home and work, and limited time. If a session feels irrelevant, they stop listening, or politely stop coming. Two ideas from adult education help you design sessions that adults value: **Malcolm Knowles' principles of andragogy** and **David Kolb's experiential learning cycle**.

blocks.name: public-discussion
blocks.alt: Adults discussing ideas together in a group
blocks.caption: Adults learn best when their own experience is part of the session.

blocks.text: Knowles: six assumptions about adult learners

head: Assumption
What it means
What you do as a trainer
rows: Adults want to know why they should learn something
Open with the real problem the session solves
Adults see themselves as responsible for their own decisions
Give choices, ask for their ideas, avoid talking down
Adults bring rich experience that is a resource
Ask them to share examples before you teach
Adults are ready to learn what helps them in their current roles
Link every topic to their business, family or community work
Adults prefer problem-centred learning over subject lists
Organise content around tasks and real cases
The strongest motivation is internal: confidence, quality of life
Show progress they can feel, not only certificates

blocks.text: Notice what this means in practice: less time reading slides, more time solving real problems. A market woman who has run a business for 15 years already knows a great deal about customers and credit. Your job is to connect new tools to what she already knows.
Kolb's experiential learning cycle
David Kolb described learning as a cycle with four stages, published in his 1984 book *Experiential Learning*. Learners can enter at any point, but a full learning experience passes through all four.

blocks.title: Kolb's experiential learning cycle
items: Concrete experience
Reflective observation
Abstract conceptualisation
Active experimentation
blocks.caption: Do something, think about it, draw a general lesson, then try it again in a new way.

items: **Concrete experience**: learners do something or experience a situation (a role play, a demonstration, a short case story).
**Reflective observation**: they look back at what happened. What did you notice? How did it feel?
**Abstract conceptualisation**: they draw out the general idea, rule or model. What does this teach us? This is where your short input fits.
**Active experimentation**: they apply the idea to a new situation or plan how they will use it at home or in business.

blocks.text: Many trainers spend almost all their time in the third stage, explaining concepts. Adults then nod politely, go home, and nothing changes. When you design every main session to include an experience, a reflection, a short concept, and an application, learning sticks far better.

blocks.title: Worked example: one 45-minute session through all four stages
blocks.context: For example, Halima is training cooperative members in Kaduna on separating business money from household money.
steps: Concrete experience (10 minutes): two volunteers act out a short role play. A trader takes money from her sales box for school fees and cooking gas, then cannot restock on market day.
Reflective observation (10 minutes): in pairs, members answer: What went wrong? Has this happened to you or someone you know?
Abstract conceptualisation (10 minutes): Halima presents one simple rule: keep two separate purses or accounts, and pay yourself a fixed amount each week from the business.
Active experimentation (15 minutes): each member decides the weekly amount she will pay herself and writes it down, then shares with a partner who will check in with her next week.
blocks.result: In 45 minutes, members moved from a familiar problem to a personal commitment. Halima only spoke for about 10 minutes, but the whole session was purposeful.

blocks.title: About 'learning styles'
blocks.text: You may hear that each person has one fixed learning style and must be taught only that way. Reviews of the research have not found good evidence for matching teaching to a single style. It is better to use variety: speaking, showing, doing and discussing in every session.
Using the cycle in a ToT

In a Training-of-Trainers, Kolb's cycle works on two levels. First, your trainees experience sessions built on the cycle as participants. Second, you pause and ask them to look at the design itself: "Which part of that session was the experience? Where did we reflect? When did I give the concept?" This makes the method visible, so they can copy it when they train others.

Good reflection questions move from what happened, to why it matters, to what next. A simple sequence many facilitators use is: **What?** (What happened? What did you notice?), **So what?** (What does this mean? Why does it matter?), and **Now what?** (What will you do differently?). These three questions fit naturally into the reflection and experimentation stages and are easy for new trainers to remember.

In the next lesson you will prepare the physical and social space where these sessions happen, because even a well-designed session fails if people cannot hear, feel unsafe, or are worried about their children outside.

takeaways: Adults need to know why, bring experience, and prefer real problems
Kolb's cycle: experience, reflect, conceptualise, experiment
Keep your own talking to a short part of each session
Use variety rather than a single 'learning style'

activity.title: Redesign one lesson with Kolb's cycle
steps: Pick a topic you would normally teach by talking (for example, how to fill a savings passbook).
Write one concrete experience you could use to open it: a role play, a story or a demonstration.
Write two reflection questions.
Write the key concept in one sentence.
Write one application task learners will complete before they leave.
activity.evidence: Your four-stage session outline written on one page or as a phone note, with estimated minutes for each stage.

lessons.title: Preparing a safe, inclusive training space
objectives: Prepare a venue and materials checklist for a community training
Agree ground rules with a group in the first session
Obtain consent before taking photos or collecting personal data
Plan for participants with disabilities, low literacy or childcare needs

blocks.text: People learn when they feel safe, comfortable and respected. A hot, crowded hall with no water, a trainer who arrives late, or a phone camera pointed at someone without permission can damage trust before you teach anything. Good trainers prepare the space as carefully as the content.

blocks.name: preparation
blocks.alt: A person preparing materials and checking a list
blocks.caption: Preparing the venue, materials and rules the day before saves you from avoidable problems.

blocks.text: Venue and logistics

items: **Seating**: arrange chairs in a horseshoe or small circles, not rows, so people can see each other and talk.
**Light, air and noise**: check fans, windows and whether a generator, church service or market noise will drown you out.
**Power**: if you need a projector or speaker, plan for power cuts. Have printed flip chart sheets as backup.
**Water and toilets**: confirm clean toilets and drinking water. Long sessions need a break every 60 to 90 minutes.
**Timing**: choose times that suit women's real schedules, for example after the morning market or after school drop-off.

blocks.text: Materials kit

A simple trainer kit works anywhere: flip chart paper, thick markers in several colours, masking tape, sticky notes or cut paper, a timer (your phone works), printed handouts, the attendance sheet, consent forms, pens for participants, and the trainer guide. Pack it the night before and tick each item.

blocks.title: Day-before readiness check
items: Venue booked and confirmed
Seating and power checked
Materials kit packed
Attendance and consent forms printed
Access and childcare planned
Co-facilitator briefed
blocks.caption: If any box is unticked the day before, fix it or change the plan.

blocks.text: Ground rules and safety

In the first 15 minutes, ask the group to suggest ground rules and write them on a flip chart. Common ones: phones on silent, one person speaks at a time, respect different views, what is shared personally stays in the room, start and end on time. Rules the group makes itself are easier to keep than rules you impose.

blocks.title: Consent for photos and personal data
blocks.text: Always ask before taking photos, and offer a clear option to say no without explanation. Use a short consent form that says what the photo or data is for and where it will be shared. Nigeria's Data Protection Act (2023) requires personal data to be collected for a clear purpose, kept secure and not shared beyond that purpose. Keep attendance lists with phone numbers in a safe place, not in a public WhatsApp group.
Inclusion from the start

items: **Language**: agree in advance whether to train in English, Pidgin, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or another local language, and arrange an interpreter if needed.
**Literacy**: use pictures, symbols, demonstrations and oral summaries so women who read little can fully take part.
**Disability**: choose a ground floor venue where possible, seat people with hearing or sight difficulties near the front, and ask privately what support each person needs.
**Childcare**: if mothers will bring babies, plan a corner or a helper so they can still participate.
**Transport and cost**: be clear in the invitation about whether transport is refunded, so nobody is embarrassed on the day.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a venue problem the day before
blocks.context: For example, Bisi is running a two-day ToT for 20 women leaders in a church hall in Ibadan. On her readiness check the evening before, she finds problems.
steps: The hall has rows of fixed benches. She arranges to use the smaller side room with movable plastic chairs and sets up four circles of five.
There is no generator on weekdays. She drops the projector plan and prepares six flip chart sheets with the key diagrams instead.
Two participants use walking sticks. She confirms the side room is on the ground floor with no steps.
Three women said they will bring babies. She asks a youth volunteer to supervise a play mat in the corner where mothers can see their children.
She counts printed consent forms: 20 needed, plus five spare.
blocks.result: On the day, the session starts on time, everyone can see and move, and nobody is excluded. Bisi notes the changes in her trainer log for next time.

blocks.text: The first 15 minutes

The opening shapes the whole day. Arrive at least 45 minutes early to set up, so you can greet people at the door rather than arranging chairs while they wait. Start with a short welcome, introductions that link to the topic (for example, "Say your name and one thing you sell"), the purpose of the day, the agenda with break times, and the ground rules. Keep the attendance sheet near the door, and explain the consent form before anyone signs it, reading it aloud for those who prefer.

blocks.title: Electrical and crowd safety
blocks.text: Check extension cables for damage, keep them away from walkways and water, and do not overload one socket with a projector, speaker and phone chargers. Know where the exits are, keep them clear, and do not pack more people into a room than it can safely hold.
As a ToT trainer, you will teach these same preparation habits to your trainees. Include a readiness checklist in their trainer guide so every local session starts well.

takeaways: Prepare the venue, power backup and materials the day before
Let the group create its own ground rules
Get clear consent before photos or collecting personal data
Plan for language, literacy, disability and childcare from the start

activity.title: Make your readiness kit
steps: Write a materials checklist for a one-day training of 20 people.
Draft a five-line consent statement for photos and contact details.
List three inclusion needs likely in your community and how you will meet each one.
Visit or call one possible venue and check seating, power, toilets and access.
activity.evidence: Your completed checklist and consent statement, plus notes or a photo from the venue check.

quiz.q: Ngozi trains 12 trainers. Each trainer agrees to run 3 sessions of 20 participants. What is the planned reach?
quiz.explain: Reach is trainers x sessions x participants per session: 12 x 3 x 20 = 720.

quiz.q: Which step best reduces dilution in a cascade?
options: Making the ToT larger so more people attend
Giving each trainer a written guide and practice teaching with feedback during the ToT
Letting each trainer change the content as she likes
Choosing trainers mainly by title or position
quiz.explain: A shared written guide plus practice and feedback keeps core messages consistent and builds trainer skill, which is how dilution is reduced.

quiz.q: In Kolb's cycle, what normally comes straight after a role play (concrete experience)?
quiz.explain: After the experience, learners reflect on what happened before drawing general lessons.

quiz.q: A trainer opens with a 40-minute lecture on budgeting and gets bored faces. Which Knowles principle is she most clearly ignoring?
options: Adults bring experience and prefer problem-centred learning
Adults need certificates to be motivated
Adults prefer long theory before practice
quiz.explain: Adults want problem-centred learning that uses their experience. Starting with their real budgeting problems would engage them.

quiz.q: During a session you want a photo for the funder's report. What should you do?
options: Take the photo quietly so nobody is uncomfortable
Post it in the group first and remove it if someone complains
Explain the purpose, ask for consent, and let anyone opt out without giving a reason
Only photograph people at the back
quiz.explain: Consent must be informed and freely given before the photo is taken, with a real option to say no.

quiz.q: The venue has no generator and your session depends on slides. What is the best preparation?
options: Prepare flip chart versions of the key visuals as a backup
Ask participants to read the slides on their phones
quiz.explain: Flip charts work without power and keep your key visuals available.

modules.title: Design and Delivery: From Needs to a Live Session
modules.overview: This module turns principles into a real training. You will use the ADDIE model and a short needs analysis to write SMART objectives with Bloom's verbs, build a session plan with timings, and practise facilitation through a microteaching cycle with structured feedback.

lessons.title: Design with ADDIE: needs analysis and SMART objectives
objectives: Describe the five phases of the ADDIE model
Carry out a quick training needs analysis with a small group
Write SMART learning objectives using Bloom's action verbs
Choose the right Bloom's level for what learners must do after training

blocks.text: Most weak trainings start with the question "What do I want to talk about?" Strong trainings start with "What must people be able to do afterwards, and what is stopping them now?" The **ADDIE model** gives you a clear order for answering that question. It is one of the most widely used frameworks in instructional design.

blocks.name: process
blocks.alt: A person arranging steps of a process
blocks.caption: ADDIE moves you step by step from a real need to a tested training.

head: Phase
Key question
What you produce
rows: Who are the learners, what gap exists, and is training the right solution?
Needs analysis notes and a short learner profile
What must learners be able to do, and how will we check?
What materials and activities do we need?
Trainer guide, handouts, case stories, test
How do we deliver it well?
Did it work, and what will we improve?

blocks.text: Quick needs analysis

Analysis does not need to be expensive. Talk to five to ten future participants and two or three people who know their work (a cooperative chair, a market leader, a health worker). Ask what tasks they find hard, what mistakes happen often, and what they already do well. Also ask a hard question: **is training the real solution?** If women cannot save because there is no safe place to keep money, a session on saving will not fix that. Training fixes gaps in knowledge and skill, not missing tools or money.
Bloom's taxonomy: choosing the right level

Benjamin Bloom and colleagues published a taxonomy of learning objectives in 1956. A revised version by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl (2001) uses six levels, from simple recall to creating something new. Each level has action verbs you can observe.

blocks.title: Revised Bloom's taxonomy (base to top)
items: Remember
Understand
Apply
Analyse
Evaluate
Create
blocks.caption: Higher levels build on lower ones; most practical trainings should reach at least Apply.

head: Level
Observable verbs
Example in a savings group training
rows: List the five rules of the group
Explain why loans are recorded in the passbook
Calculate interest on a 20,000 naira loan at the group rate
Identify why a member's records do not balance
Decide whether a loan request meets the group rules
Design a repayment plan for a member who fell behind

blocks.title: Avoid unmeasurable verbs
blocks.text: Verbs like "know", "understand", "appreciate" or "be aware of" cannot be observed. You cannot see someone "know" something. Replace them with what she will say, write, calculate or do.
Making objectives SMART

A good learning objective is **Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound**. In training, the time part is usually "by the end of the session". A simple formula: **By the end of [time], participants will be able to [Bloom's verb] [task] [to what standard].**

blocks.title: Worked example: from vague aim to SMART objectives
blocks.context: For example, Chioma is designing a half-day training for 25 women who sell cooked food at a motor park in Owerri. Her first draft aim was: "Participants will understand food hygiene."
steps: Analysis: she talks to eight sellers and the park's welfare officer. The main gaps: not washing hands after handling money, keeping cooked food uncovered, and reusing dirty water.
She checks that training is the right fix: soap and covers are affordable, so the gap is habits and knowledge, not missing tools.
Objective 1 (Apply): By the end of the session, participants will be able to demonstrate correct hand washing with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds.
Objective 2 (Understand): By the end of the session, participants will be able to explain two ways uncovered food becomes contaminated.
Objective 3 (Create): By the end of the session, each participant will be able to draw up a three-step daily hygiene routine for her own stall.
blocks.result: Each objective is observable and can be checked before the women leave: a hand washing demonstration, a short verbal explanation, and a written or drawn routine.

blocks.text: Write objectives before you write any content or activities. Then, in the Development phase, check every handout and activity against them. If an activity does not help learners reach an objective, it is decoration. Objectives also become your test questions later: an objective that says "calculate interest" needs a test item where learners actually calculate interest.
In a ToT, share your objectives with trainees and ask them to check each local session against the same objectives, so every level of the cascade aims at the same result.
Three to five objectives are enough for a half-day session. More than that usually means you are trying to cover too much, which is one of the most common reasons community trainings run over time.

takeaways: ADDIE: Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation
Check that training is the real solution before designing it
Use observable Bloom's verbs, never 'know' or 'understand' alone
SMART objective formula: by when, able to verb, task, standard

activity.title: Run a mini needs analysis
steps: Choose a training topic for a group you can reach.
Ask five future participants three questions: what is hard, what goes wrong often, what do you already do well?
Write one sentence on whether training is the right solution, and why.
Write three SMART objectives, each at a stated Bloom's level.
activity.evidence: Your interview notes (no names needed) and three SMART objectives labelled with their Bloom's level.

lessons.title: Building a session plan with timings
objectives: Structure a session into opening, activities, input, practice and close
Allocate realistic minutes to each part of a session
Write a session plan that another trainer could follow
Build in buffer time and a plan B

blocks.text: A **session plan** is the trainer's map. It lists each part of the session, how long it takes, what the trainer does, what participants do, and what materials are needed. In a ToT, session plans are essential: they are what your trainees carry home, and they are your best protection against dilution.

blocks.name: schedule
blocks.alt: A person planning a schedule on a calendar
blocks.caption: A session plan turns objectives into a timed sequence anyone can follow.

blocks.text: The parts of a strong session

items: **Opening (about 10 percent of time)**: welcome, purpose, objectives in plain words, link to what learners already know.
**Experience or activity**: a role play, demonstration, case story or problem that gets people involved early.
**Reflection and discussion**: pairs or small groups talk about what happened and share with the room.
**Short input**: the key concept, rule or method, usually 10 to 15 minutes at a time.
**Practice**: learners apply the method themselves, with the trainer moving around to help.
**Check and close**: a quick check against the objectives, a summary, and one action each person will take.

blocks.text: Plan **one objective per main block**, and check each block with a question: does this activity help participants reach the objective? If not, cut it, even if it is interesting.

blocks.title: A two-hour session at a glance
items: 0:00 Welcome and objectives
0:15 Role play and reflection
0:45 Short input
1:00 Group practice
1:40 Check and close
blocks.caption: Input is short and sits between experience and practice, as in Kolb's cycle.

blocks.text: A session plan format

head: Time
Activity and objective
Trainer does
Participants do
Materials
rows: Greets, shares objectives on flip chart
Practice: record a day of sales (Objective 2)
Fill in practice sheet in pairs

blocks.title: Worked example: fitting content into the time you really have
blocks.context: For example, Fatima has a three-hour slot (180 minutes) with a women's cooperative in Kano. Her first plan has 230 minutes of activities.
steps: She first protects realistic overhead: 15 minutes for late arrivals and settling, and a 20-minute break. That leaves 145 minutes of teaching time.

She keeps her three objectives and lists every activity under one of them. Two activities support no objective: a long history of cooperatives (25 minutes) and a second icebreaker (15 minutes). She cuts both.
Now the plan is 190 minutes, still 45 over her 145. She shortens her input on record keeping from 35 to 15 minutes and uses a printed handout instead.
She reduces group reports from 30 to 15 minutes by asking only two groups to report and others to add anything new.
Final plan: 130 minutes of activities, leaving a 15-minute buffer for questions or delays.
blocks.result: Fatima's plan now fits 145 minutes with a 15-minute buffer, covers all three objectives, and keeps practice time intact, which is where most learning happens.

blocks.title: Always have a plan B
blocks.text: Mark one activity in your plan as optional, so you can drop it if you run late. Mark another as a stretch activity in case a fast group finishes early. Write both into the trainer guide so your trainees can do the same.

Timing estimates improve with experience. After each session, write the actual time each block took beside the planned time. After two or three sessions you will plan much more accurately, and you can share these real timings with the trainers you train.
Energy across the day

Attention drops after a heavy lunch and late in the afternoon. Put active work, such as practice, role plays and gallery walks, in those slots, and keep short inputs for the morning when people are fresh. A quick energiser of two or three minutes (standing up, a clapping game, a quick quiz) can rescue a tired room, but choose energisers that suit the age, culture and physical ability of the group. Nobody should feel embarrassed or excluded.

For a full-day ToT, repeat the same structure across several sessions and end the day with a short review: what did we learn today, what is still unclear, and what will we do tomorrow? Write the unclear points on a flip chart and start the next morning by answering them.

blocks.title: Keep the language plain
blocks.text: Write session plans in the language and style your trainees will use. If a trainer will deliver in Hausa or Pidgin, translate the key messages and questions in advance, rather than asking her to translate on the spot.

takeaways: A session plan shows time, activity, trainer action, participant action and materials
Every activity must support an objective, or it goes
Protect settling time, breaks and a buffer
Record actual timings to improve future plans

activity.title: Write a two-hour session plan
steps: Take the three SMART objectives from the previous lesson.
Draft a session plan in the five-column format, with timings for every block.
Check that each block supports one objective and remove any that do not.
Mark one optional activity and one stretch activity.
Ask a friend or colleague to read it and tell you if she could deliver it without your help.
activity.evidence: Your completed session plan (photo or typed) and one sentence of feedback from the person who read it.

lessons.title: Facilitation techniques, microteaching and feedback
objectives: Use at least five participatory facilitation techniques
Ask open questions and manage dominant or quiet participants
Run a microteaching cycle in a ToT
Give specific, kind and useful feedback using a structured model

blocks.text: A facilitator makes learning easier. She does not stand at the front holding all the answers. She designs activities, asks good questions, manages time and energy, and helps the group find and test answers. This is a skill, and like any skill it improves with practice and feedback.

blocks.name: feedback
blocks.caption: Practice teaching followed by specific feedback is the heart of any good ToT.

blocks.text: Facilitation techniques and when to use them

head: Technique
How it works
Best for
rows: Pairs or threes talk for 3 to 5 minutes on one question
Waking up a quiet room, getting everyone to speak
Group shouts out ideas, trainer writes all, no judging until later
Trainer shows a skill step by step, then learners practise
Practical skills like hand washing or filling a ledger
Volunteers act out a realistic situation
Communication, negotiation, sensitive topics at a safe distance
Groups analyse a short realistic story and decide what to do
Groups post flip charts on walls and rotate to comment
Sharing group work without long reports

blocks.text: Asking good questions

Closed questions ("Did you understand?") get a yes and tell you nothing. Open questions start with what, how, why or tell me about: "What would you do if a member missed two repayments?" After asking, **wait**. Count silently to five before rephrasing. Silence gives quieter people time to think.

items: **Dominant participant**: thank her, then say "Let us hear from someone who has not spoken yet." Give her a role, such as timekeeper.
**Quiet participant**: use pairs first, so she can rehearse with one person. Ask her group, not her alone, to report.
**Off-topic question**: write it on a "parking lot" sheet and promise to return to it at the break.
**Disagreement**: welcome it, ask each side for their reasons, and link back to the evidence or the objective.

blocks.text: Microteaching

**Microteaching** is a short practice teaching session, usually 10 to 15 minutes, delivered to a small group of fellow trainees who then give feedback. It is the most important part of a ToT, because trainers learn to teach by teaching, not by listening to talks about teaching.

blocks.title: The microteaching cycle
items: Plan a short segment
Teach to peers
Receive feedback
Re-plan
Re-teach
blocks.caption: Teaching the same segment twice, with feedback in between, shows each trainer how much she can improve.

blocks.text: Giving useful feedback

Feedback should be **specific, about behaviour (not personality), balanced and actionable**. Two simple models work well in community settings. The first is **What went well / Even better if**: name two things that worked and one clear improvement. The second is **Situation-Behaviour-Impact (SBI)**, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership: describe when it happened, what the person did, and the effect it had.

blocks.title: Worked example: a microteaching round in a ToT
blocks.context: For example, in a ToT in Jos, Rahila teaches a 12-minute segment on filling a savings passbook to five peers. Her co-trainer Esther leads the feedback.
steps: Rahila states her objective: "By the end, you will be able to record a deposit in the passbook correctly."
She demonstrates once, then asks everyone to record a 5,000 naira deposit. Two peers make mistakes in the balance column.
Feedback, what went well: "Your objective was clear, and you got everyone practising within five minutes."
Feedback, SBI: "When you checked the practice sheets (situation), you corrected the errors yourself (behaviour), so the two learners did not find out why they were wrong (impact)."
Even better if: "Ask the learner to check her balance against the sample first, then explain."
Rahila re-plans and re-teaches the next day. This time both struggling peers find their own errors.
blocks.result: Rahila improves one specific skill, guiding learners to correct their own mistakes, in under 30 minutes of practice and feedback.

blocks.text: Receiving feedback is a skill too. Teach trainees to listen without defending themselves, write down what they hear, ask a clarifying question if needed ("Can you give me an example?"), and thank the person. They then choose one or two points to work on, rather than trying to fix everything at once. In a ToT, model this yourself by asking participants for feedback on your own sessions at the end of each day.

When planning microteaching, divide trainees into groups of four to six with one experienced trainer or a trained peer as the feedback lead. Give each trainee a different segment of the real curriculum, so the whole training is rehearsed by the group, and keep strict time: about 10 to 15 minutes teaching and 10 minutes feedback each.

blocks.title: Feedback rules to agree in the ToT
blocks.text: The person who taught speaks first about what she noticed. Peers then give one strength and one improvement each. No one comments on voice, accent, appearance or dress. Feedback is about teaching behaviour only.

takeaways: Choose techniques that match the objective: demonstrate skills, role play communication
Ask open questions and wait at least five seconds
Microteaching: plan, teach, feedback, re-plan, re-teach
Feedback is specific, about behaviour, balanced and actionable

activity.title: Run and record a microteach
steps: Choose a 10-minute segment from your session plan.
Teach it to three to five people (family, friends or group members).
Ask each person for one 'went well' and one 'even better if'.
Re-plan the segment based on the feedback and teach it again, or write exactly what you will change.
Write a short reflection: what changed between the first and second attempt?
activity.evidence: The feedback notes from your observers and your short reflection. A short video or photo is optional, with everyone's consent.

quiz.q: Women in a community cannot save because there is no safe place to keep money. In ADDIE's Analysis phase, what should the trainer conclude?
options: A longer savings training is needed
Training alone may not solve this; a safe savings option is also needed
Skip analysis and go straight to development
Teach Bloom's taxonomy to the women
quiz.explain: Analysis checks whether training is the right solution. Training fixes knowledge and skill gaps, not missing tools or services.

quiz.q: Which learning objective is best written?
options: Participants will know about record keeping
Participants will appreciate the value of savings
By the end of the session, participants will be able to calculate their weekly profit from a sample sales record
quiz.explain: It has a time frame, an observable Bloom's verb (calculate), a task, and can be checked.

quiz.q: A trainee must decide whether a member's loan request follows the group's rules. Which Bloom's level is this?
quiz.explain: Judging a request against criteria and justifying the decision is Evaluate.

quiz.q: Fatima has 120 minutes. She needs 10 minutes settling, a 15-minute break and wants a 10-minute buffer. How many minutes remain for planned activities?
quiz.explain: 120 - 10 - 15 - 10 = 85 minutes for activities.

quiz.q: One participant answers every question before others can speak. What is a good first response?
options: Ignore her raised hand for the rest of the day
Thank her, invite someone who has not spoken yet, and give her a role such as timekeeper
quiz.explain: This respects her while opening space for others, and channels her energy usefully.

quiz.q: Which is an example of SBI feedback?
options: When you introduced the role play, you gave clear instructions, so every group started quickly
quiz.explain: It names the situation, the specific behaviour and its impact.

modules.title: Quality, Ethics and Evaluation
modules.overview: Running a training once is not enough; it has to be good every time, safe for everyone, and proven to work. This module covers quality standards and common mistakes, ethics and safeguarding in community training, and how to evaluate results with Kirkpatrick's four levels and report them clearly.

lessons.title: Quality standards and common training mistakes
objectives: Recognise the most common mistakes in community trainings and ToTs
Use a session observation checklist to judge quality
Explain fidelity to the trainer guide and when adaptation is acceptable
Plan co-facilitation so two trainers support each other

blocks.text: Quality in training means participants reach the objectives, feel respected, and leave able to do something they could not do before. It does not mean beautiful slides or a famous speaker. In a cascade, quality also means that a session delivered by a new trainer in a village is close to the session delivered by the master trainer.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: An observation checklist turns 'it went well' into evidence you can act on.

blocks.text: Common mistakes and their fixes

head: Mistake
What you see
Fix
rows: Trainer rushes, skips practice, runs over time
Three to five objectives per half day; cut what does not serve them
Trainer talks for most of the session, few questions
Follow Kolb's cycle; input in short blocks
Participants watch but never try the skill
Plan practice time first, then fit the input around it
Use local words and examples, explain any term once
Start on time, break every 60 to 90 minutes
Trainer asks 'any questions?' and moves on
End each block with a quick task or question tied to the objective

blocks.text: Fidelity and adaptation

**Fidelity** means delivering a training as designed: the same key messages, activities and checks. In a cascade, fidelity matters because a trainer who changes the key messages may spread wrong information. But some adaptation is healthy: changing a case story so it fits farmers rather than traders, or delivering in Yoruba instead of English.

A useful rule for your trainer guide: mark content as **core** (must not change: facts, safety rules, key steps, the test) or **flexible** (can adapt: examples, names in stories, energisers, language). Trainers then know what they may adjust.

blocks.title: Weak session vs strong session
items: Weak session
Strong session
left: Trainer talks most of the time
right: Participants active most of the time
Ends on time with a check
blocks.caption: Most quality problems can be seen by an observer in the first hour.

blocks.text: Observing a session
A simple observation checklist lets a master trainer or peer give fair, consistent feedback. Score each item 0 (not seen), 1 (partly) or 2 (fully). Keep it short enough to complete while watching.

items: Objectives shared in plain language at the start
Participants actively involved within the first 15 minutes
Core messages delivered accurately
Participants practise the skill
Open questions used, and quiet people included
Learning checked against the objectives
Session ends on time with a clear action

blocks.title: Worked example: using an observation score
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma, a master trainer, observes Grace's first local session on savings group rules in a village near Abakaliki, using the seven-item checklist (maximum 14 points).
steps: Scores: objectives 2, early involvement 1, core messages 2, practice 0, questions 1, check 1, ending 2. Total 9 out of 14.
Ifeoma notes the main gap: the group never practised filling the passbook, because Grace spent extra time on the history of savings groups.
Feedback using What went well / Even better if: "Your key rules were accurate and clear. Even better if you cut the history and give 20 minutes to passbook practice."
They agree that the history section becomes flexible (optional) in the trainer guide, and practice becomes core.
At Grace's next session, Ifeoma checks by phone with two participants, who describe filling in the passbook themselves.
blocks.result: One observation found a fixable gap, improved Grace's practice, and led to a clearer trainer guide for every trainer in the cascade.

blocks.text: Co-facilitation

Pairing trainers improves quality. Before the session, agree who leads which block, who keeps time, and a signal for "we are running late". During the session, the supporting trainer watches the room, helps groups and notes questions. After the session, take 10 minutes to debrief: what worked, what to change. New trainers learn fast when paired with experienced ones.

Quality also depends on who is selected as a trainer. Agree selection criteria with the community or organisation in advance, write them down and apply them openly. When people see that trainers are chosen for knowledge, communication skills and commitment rather than family or political ties, they trust the training more and participants take it more seriously.

Finally, quality needs time. A ToT squeezed into one afternoon cannot give each trainer practice and feedback. When planning with partners, protect enough days for the content, microteaching for every trainer, and a short session on how to use the evaluation tools, even if that means training fewer trainers at first.

blocks.title: Keep a trainer log
blocks.text: After every session, write the date, place, number of participants, what went well, what you would change, and actual timings. A notebook or phone note is enough. Over time it becomes powerful evidence of your growth.

takeaways: Quality means participants reach the objectives, not that slides look good
Mark trainer guide content as core or flexible
Observe with a short scored checklist and give specific feedback
Co-facilitation and a trainer log raise quality fast

activity.title: Build and test an observation checklist
steps: Adapt the seven-item checklist to your own training topic.
Ask someone to observe one session or microteach you deliver, using the checklist.
Total the score and pick the lowest item as your improvement target.
Mark three parts of your session plan as core and three as flexible.
activity.evidence: The completed checklist with scores, your chosen improvement target, and your core and flexible list.

lessons.title: Ethics, inclusion and safeguarding in community training
objectives: Apply the principle of do no harm when planning a training
Handle personal stories, personal data and money transparently
Make sessions accessible to women with low literacy or disabilities
Respond correctly when a participant discloses harm

blocks.text: Trainers hold power. Participants may look up to you, depend on you for transport refunds or certificates, or share personal stories during discussions. With that power comes responsibility. Ethical training protects participants, protects your reputation, and protects the organisation you work with.

blocks.name: security
blocks.alt: A shield protecting a person and their information
blocks.caption: Protecting participants' safety, dignity and data is part of the trainer's job.

blocks.text: Do no harm

Before a training, ask: could anything in this session put someone at risk? Examples: a discussion of money that makes a woman's husband suspicious, a role play about conflict that reopens painful memories, or a group photo that reveals someone's location. Design to reduce these risks, for example by using fictional case stories instead of asking for personal experiences on sensitive topics.
Confidentiality and personal data

items: Agree in the ground rules that personal stories shared in the room are not repeated outside it.
Collect only the personal data you need. If you only need numbers for a report, do not collect home addresses.
Explain why you are collecting phone numbers or test scores and who will see them.
Store attendance lists and forms securely: a locked bag or folder, or a password-protected phone or file.
Report results as totals or averages, not named individuals, unless someone has given permission.

blocks.text: These habits match the principles of Nigeria's Data Protection Act (2023), enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission: personal data should be collected for a clear purpose, limited to what is necessary, kept secure, and not used for other purposes without consent.
Money and transparency

Transport refunds, lunch and materials are common sources of conflict and mistrust. State clearly in the invitation what will be provided. Pay or refund in the same way for everyone, record every payment with a signature or transfer receipt, and never ask participants for money to receive a certificate unless this was openly agreed in advance. Where possible, use bank transfer or a mobile money app so there is a record.
Inclusion

blocks.title: Inclusion check before every session
items: Language agreed and interpreter ready
Pictures for low-literacy learners
Accessible venue and seating
Childcare or baby corner planned
Private way to share needs
Fair, recorded refunds
blocks.caption: If you cannot tick an item, decide how you will close the gap before the day.

blocks.text: Inclusion is not only about who is invited, but whether each person can fully take part. Use oral instructions as well as written ones, read handouts aloud, and use symbols or colours on forms. For evaluation, replace written tests with picture-based questions or short oral checks when literacy is low. Ask privately, for example on the registration form, whether anyone needs support to participate.

blocks.title: If someone discloses harm
blocks.text: Sometimes a participant shares that she or her child is being harmed. Listen calmly, do not push for details, and do not promise to keep a secret you may need to report. Thank her for telling you, explain what you can and cannot do, and follow your organisation's safeguarding procedure by informing the named safeguarding focal person promptly. Never investigate on your own. Before any training, find out who that focal person is and which local support services exist.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning an ethical, inclusive session
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is preparing a ToT on household budgeting for 20 women in a community near Maiduguri. Several participants do not read, and the topic touches family finances.
steps: She replaces 'share your own family budget' with a fictional case story of a woman called Laraba, so nobody has to reveal personal income.
She designs a picture-based budget sheet using symbols for food, school fees, transport and savings, so women who do not read can use it.
Her registration form asks only for name, phone number and any support needs, and explains the data is for follow-up calls only.

She budgets 1,500 naira per person for transport (an approximate local figure for this example), pays by transfer where possible, and records cash payments with a thumbprint where someone cannot sign.
She confirms with her organisation who the safeguarding focal person is and writes the contact in her trainer guide.
blocks.result: Zainab's session protects privacy, includes non-readers fully, keeps money transparent and is ready if a sensitive disclosure happens.

blocks.text: Respect also shows in small things: using people's preferred names and titles, not singling out anyone's mistakes in front of the group, scheduling around prayer times and market days, and making sure older women and younger women both get a chance to speak. These habits make the training room a place where women feel safe enough to try new skills and admit what they do not yet know.

When you train other trainers, include these ethics practices in the ToT itself, through a short case discussion such as: "A participant asks you to lend her money. What do you do?" Practising these situations before they happen builds good judgement.

takeaways: Do no harm: use fictional cases for sensitive topics
Collect minimal personal data, explain why, and store it securely
Make money handling transparent and recorded
Know your safeguarding focal person before every training

activity.title: Run an ethics and inclusion review
steps: Read your session plan and list any activity that could cause harm or embarrassment.
Rewrite one of them using a fictional case or a safer method.
Adapt one handout or evaluation question for low-literacy learners using pictures or an oral format.
Find out who the safeguarding focal person is for your group or organisation and note their contact.
activity.evidence: Your before-and-after activity, the adapted handout or question, and the safeguarding contact recorded in your trainer guide.

lessons.title: Evaluating training with Kirkpatrick's four levels
objectives: Describe Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation
Design a simple pre-test and post-test and calculate the change
Plan a follow-up check of behaviour after training
Write a one-page evaluation report

blocks.text: How do you know your training worked? "People enjoyed it" is a start, but it is not proof that anything changed. **Kirkpatrick's four levels**, first described by Donald Kirkpatrick in the late 1950s, are the most widely used framework for evaluating training. Each level answers a different question.

blocks.name: data-reports
blocks.alt: A person reviewing charts and reports
blocks.caption: Simple numbers from tests and follow-up calls show whether training made a difference.

blocks.title: Kirkpatrick's four levels (base to top)
items: Level 1: Reaction
Level 2: Learning
Level 3: Behaviour
Level 4: Results
blocks.caption: Each level is harder to measure than the one below, and closer to real impact.

head: Level
Question
Simple tool
When
rows: Did participants find it useful, relevant and engaging?
Short feedback form or smiley-face scale
Did knowledge, skills or confidence improve?
Are they using it in real life?
Follow-up call, visit, record book check
Did it lead to the outcomes we wanted?

blocks.text: Level 1 and 2 tools

For reaction, keep the form short: three to five questions such as "How useful was today for your work?" on a 1 to 5 scale, plus "What will you use first?" and "What should we change?" For low-literacy groups, use smiley faces and ask the open questions orally.

For learning, use the **same short test before and after** the session, five to ten questions linked directly to your objectives. Skill objectives are best checked by watching a demonstration with a simple checklist. Calculate the average score before and after, and the change.

blocks.title: Worked example: calculating learning gain and follow-up
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a record keeping training for 20 traders in Onitsha with a 10-question pre-test and post-test, and follows up six weeks later.
steps: Pre-test: the 20 scores add up to 80, so the average is 80 / 20 = 4.0 out of 10 (40 percent).
Post-test: the scores add up to 160, so the average is 160 / 20 = 8.0 out of 10 (80 percent).
Change: 8.0 - 4.0 = 4.0 points, an increase of 40 percentage points. 17 of 20 traders scored 7 or above after training, compared with 2 before.
Reaction: average usefulness rating 4.6 out of 5. Most common request: more practice time.
Behaviour, six weeks later: she calls all 20 and reaches 18. Of these, 12 say they record sales daily, and she sees photos of record books from 9 of them.
blocks.result: Ngozi can report strong learning (40 to 80 percent) and early behaviour change (12 of the 18 reached are recording daily), while honestly noting that 9 confirmations are backed by photos and the rest are self-reported.

blocks.title: Be honest about what the numbers show
blocks.text: A higher post-test score shows learning, not business growth. Self-reported behaviour may be higher than real behaviour. State how many people you reached at follow-up and how you checked. Honest reports build more trust with funders than impressive claims.
Behaviour and results

Level 3 is where most trainings fall silent, yet it is often what funders and communities care about most. Plan it before training starts: decide what behaviour you expect, how you will check it (call, visit, photo of a record book), and when. Level 4 results, such as increased group savings or fewer food hygiene complaints, usually need records kept over months and are influenced by many factors besides training, so describe your contribution carefully rather than claiming the training alone caused them.
A one-page evaluation report

items: **What**: training title, dates, place, trainers, number of participants (and how many were women, youth or persons with disabilities if relevant).
**Objectives**: the three to five learning objectives.
**Results by level**: reaction average, pre and post averages, behaviour follow-up findings.
**What worked and what we will change**: two or three points each.
**Evidence and limits**: how data was collected, how many were followed up, what was self-reported.

blocks.text: Keep evaluation light enough that trainers will actually do it. A five-question reaction form, a ten-question test and three follow-up questions by phone are enough for most community trainings. Agree in advance who collects the forms, who enters the scores (a simple spreadsheet or exercise book is fine), and when the report is due. In a cascade, use exactly the same tools at every level so you can compare results between trainers and spot where quality is dropping.
Share results back with participants too. Telling a group "most of you improved from 4 to 8 out of 10" builds confidence and encourages them to keep using the skill.

takeaways: Kirkpatrick: reaction, learning, behaviour, results
Use the same short test before and after and compare averages
Plan behaviour follow-up before the training starts
Report honestly, including limits and self-reported data

activity.title: Build your evaluation kit
steps: Write a five-question reaction form, with a smiley-face version for low-literacy groups.
Write a pre-test and post-test of five to ten questions linked to your objectives.
Decide one behaviour you will check at follow-up, how and when.
Draft the headings of your one-page evaluation report.
activity.evidence: Your reaction form, test, follow-up plan and report template, saved as photos or a document.

quiz.q: A trainer guide says safety steps and the test are 'core'. A trainer changes a case story from traders to farmers. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes, examples and stories are flexible content that can be adapted
Only if the master trainer is present
Yes, and she may also change the safety steps
quiz.explain: Examples are flexible. Core content such as facts, safety rules, key steps and the test must stay the same.

quiz.q: An observer scores a session 8 out of 14. The lowest item is 'participants practise the skill' (0). What is the best feedback?
options: Even better if you give time for participants to practise the skill, for example by shortening the input
Make the session longer by an hour
quiz.explain: Feedback should target the specific lowest item and suggest a concrete, achievable fix.

quiz.q: During a break, a participant tells you her child is being harmed at home. What should you do?
options: Visit the family yourself to investigate
Listen calmly, avoid pushing for details, explain what you must do, and inform the safeguarding focal person
Ask her to share it with the whole group
quiz.explain: Listen, do not promise secrecy, do not investigate yourself, and follow the safeguarding procedure promptly.

quiz.q: Pre-test scores for 15 participants total 60 out of 150. Post-test scores total 120. What is the change in average score?
quiz.explain: 60 / 15 = 4.0 and 120 / 15 = 8.0, so the average rose from 4 to 8 out of 10.

quiz.q: Six weeks after training, you call participants to see if they keep daily sales records. Which Kirkpatrick level is this?
quiz.explain: Checking whether people apply the skill in real life is Level 3, Behaviour.

quiz.q: Which data practice follows good ethics and Nigeria's Data Protection Act principles?
options: Posting the attendance list with phone numbers in a public group
Collecting only what is needed, explaining the purpose, and storing it securely
Sharing named test scores with the community
quiz.explain: Purpose, minimal collection and secure storage are core data protection principles.

modules.title: Portfolio, Partnerships and Impact
modules.overview: In this final module you turn your work into a complete training package and portfolio, learn to present its value to partners such as NGOs, churches, cooperatives and employers, and finish with an honest certification checklist and a 90-day plan for training and mentoring others.

lessons.title: Building your training package and ToT portfolio
objectives: List the components of a complete training package
Pilot a training and improve it from evidence
Organise a portfolio that proves your competence as a trainer
Prepare materials that another trainer can use without you

blocks.text: A trainer who can deliver a good session is valuable. A trainer who can hand over a complete, tested training package that others deliver well is even more valuable. That package, plus evidence of how it worked, becomes your **ToT portfolio** and your capstone for this course.

blocks.name: portfolio-feedback
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a portfolio of work with feedback notes
blocks.caption: Your portfolio shows not just what you planned, but what happened and what you improved.

blocks.text: What goes into a training package

head: Component
What it contains
Who uses it
rows: Purpose, objectives, session plans with timings, key messages marked core or flexible, facilitation notes, readiness checklist
Handouts, picture sheets, practice forms, written in plain language
Role cards, case stories, sample records, flip chart templates
Reaction form, pre and post test, observation checklist, follow-up questions
Attendance sheet, consent form, payment record

blocks.text: A good test of your trainer guide: give it to someone who did not attend your ToT and ask her to explain how she would run the first session. Every place she hesitates or asks a question is a gap in the guide.
Pilot before you scale

The Implementation and Evaluation phases of ADDIE are where you learn whether the design works. Run a **pilot**: deliver the training once to a small real group, collect all your evaluation data, and revise the package before training other trainers on it. Mistakes are cheap in a pilot and expensive in a cascade.

blocks.title: From draft to tested package
items: Draft the package
Pilot with real group
Collect evaluation data
Revise the materials
Train other trainers
blocks.caption: Piloting once before scaling catches problems while they are still cheap to fix.

blocks.title: Worked example: a pilot that changed the package
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze designs a one-day training on safe storage of grains for women farmers in Benue, and pilots it with 16 women before running a ToT for 15 trainers.
steps: Pre-test average: 3.5 out of 10. Post-test average: 6.0 out of 10. Lower than her target of 7.
She looks question by question: most women still got the two questions on checking moisture wrong.
Reaction forms say the demonstration was hard to see from the back. Her own timing log shows that block ran 20 minutes short because she rushed.
She revises: the demonstration is now done in three small groups with a co-trainer, and moisture checking gets 20 more minutes of practice.
A second short pilot with 12 women gives a post-test average of 7.8 out of 10. She then finalises the trainer guide for the ToT.
blocks.result: One pilot and one revision raised the average post-test score from 6.0 to 7.8 before the material reached 15 trainers and their communities.

blocks.text: Organising your portfolio

items: **Cover page**: your name, the training title, the audience and dates.
**Needs analysis summary**: who, what gap, why training is the right solution.
**Design**: SMART objectives with Bloom's levels and the session plan.
**Materials**: the trainer guide and participant materials.
**Delivery evidence**: attendance totals, photos taken with consent, observation checklist.
**Evaluation**: reaction, pre and post results, follow-up findings, one-page report.
**Reflection**: what changed after feedback, and what you would do differently.

blocks.title: Store it so it survives
blocks.text: Keep a digital copy in Google Drive or another cloud folder, and a printed copy in a clear file. Name files clearly, for example 'Grain-storage-trainer-guide-v2'. Low-data tip: save photos at a reduced size before uploading.
Version control

Each time you revise the package, give it a new version number and date, and keep a short change list at the front of the trainer guide: what changed and why. When you run a ToT, make sure every trainer receives the same, latest version. Collect feedback from trainers after their first sessions and plan a review of the package, for example every six months, so it stays accurate and useful.

Write participant materials at a reading level that fits your group: short sentences, everyday words, one idea per line, and pictures where possible. Test a handout with two or three people from the target group and ask them to explain it back to you. If they cannot, simplify it. For groups that do not read, the trainer guide should include an oral version of each handout, and picture cards that carry the main steps.

Finally, decide who owns the package. If you created it for an organisation, agree whether they may share or adapt it, and how you will be credited. Keep your own copy of your portfolio, with permission, as evidence of your work.
A strong portfolio does not hide problems. Showing a low first score, what you changed, and the improved result is far more convincing to a partner than a perfect story with no evidence.

takeaways: A training package: trainer guide, participant materials, resources, evaluation and admin forms
Test the guide with someone who did not attend your training
Pilot and revise before training other trainers
Show problems and improvements honestly in your portfolio

activity.title: Assemble your package draft
steps: Create a folder (digital or paper) with the five package components as sections.
Place in it everything you produced in Modules 1 to 3.
Give your trainer guide to one person who has not seen it and note every question she asks.
Fix at least three gaps she found.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your organised folder, and a list of the gaps found and how you fixed them.

lessons.title: Communicating value to partners and pricing your training
objectives: Identify the stakeholders for a training and what each one cares about
Write a short training proposal for an NGO, church, cooperative or employer
Calculate a cost per participant and set a fair fee
Present evaluation results clearly and honestly

blocks.text: Good trainers are often invited to work for NGOs, faith groups, cooperatives, schools, local government programmes or private businesses. To win that work, you must explain clearly what your training will achieve, what it will cost, and how you will show results. Partners do not buy sessions; they want changes in what people can do.

blocks.name: pitching
blocks.alt: A woman presenting a proposal to a small audience
blocks.caption: A clear proposal links your training to what the partner wants to change.

blocks.text: Who cares about your training

A common planning tool is a **power and interest grid**. Place each stakeholder by how much power they have over the training (funding, permission, venue) and how interested they are in the result. This tells you how much attention to give each one.

blocks.title: Stakeholder power and interest grid
items: Keep satisfied
Manage closely
Monitor
Keep informed
axes: Interest in the training (low to high)
Power over the training (low to high)
blocks.caption: High power, high interest partners such as the funder need regular contact and clear reports.

head: Stakeholder
What they usually care about
What to show them
rows: Reach, learning results, value for money, honest reporting
Objectives, evaluation plan, budget, past results
Members' welfare, respect for values, convenience
Session times, content outline, trainer background

blocks.text: A one-page proposal

items: **The need**: two or three sentences from your needs analysis.
**What participants will be able to do**: your SMART objectives.
**How**: number of sessions, length, methods (practice, role play, demonstration), language.
**How we will know it worked**: reaction, pre and post test, follow-up check.
**Cost and what it covers**: total and per participant.
**About the trainer**: relevant experience and one result from a past training.

blocks.text: Costing a training

List every cost: venue, materials and printing, refreshments, transport refunds, co-facilitator fee, your own fee (preparation days as well as delivery days), data and phone credit for follow-up calls. Add a small contingency, often around 10 percent, for price changes. Then divide by the number of participants.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a one-day training for 25 women
blocks.context: For example, Kemi is asked by a cooperative in Abeokuta to run a one-day record keeping training for 25 members. All prices are approximate figures for illustration only; use current local prices.
steps: Venue: provided free by the cooperative, 0 naira.
Printing handouts and practice sheets: 25 x 800 = 20,000 naira.
Flip chart, markers and tape: 10,000 naira. Refreshments: 25 x 1,500 = 37,500 naira.
Co-facilitator fee: 15,000 naira. Kemi's fee for one preparation day and one delivery day: 2 x 25,000 = 50,000 naira. Follow-up calls (data and airtime): 5,000 naira.
Subtotal: 20,000 + 10,000 + 37,500 + 15,000 + 50,000 + 5,000 = 137,500 naira. Contingency of 10 percent: 13,750 naira. Total: 151,250 naira.
Cost per participant: 151,250 / 25 = 6,050 naira.
blocks.result: Kemi quotes about 151,000 naira in total, roughly 6,000 naira per participant, and shows the cooperative exactly what each amount covers.

blocks.title: Paid, partly paid or volunteer
blocks.text: Not every training will be paid. Many community sessions are voluntary. Still, cost them fully, so that partners see the real value, and so you can ask a funder or sponsor to cover the costs. When payment is involved, use a transfer or a payment link such as Paystack and always issue a receipt.
Building trust with partners

Agree in writing, even in a short email or WhatsApp message, what you will deliver, the dates, the number of participants, the payment terms and the report you will send. Send your report on time, even when results are mixed. Partners return to trainers who are reliable and honest, and a satisfied partner often recommends you to others.

Different partners need different levels of detail. A funder may want a full budget table and evaluation plan; a women's fellowship leader may only need the dates, the topic, what members will be able to do, and what it will cost. Prepare a one-page version and a short three-line version for WhatsApp, and offer the full detail on request.

If a partner offers less money than your budget, do not simply cut your fee in silence. Show the options: fewer participants, fewer printed materials, a shorter session, or a sponsor to cover part of the cost. Protect practice time and follow-up, because those produce the results the partner wants to see.

When you present results, lead with the change in what people can do, then the numbers that show it, then the evidence and its limits. For example: "After training, 17 of 20 traders could complete a daily sales record correctly, up from 2 before. Six weeks later, 12 of 18 reached said they record daily, and 9 shared photos." That is clear, specific and honest.

takeaways: Partners want changes in ability and behaviour, not just sessions
Map stakeholders by power and interest
Cost everything, including preparation and follow-up, plus a contingency
Present results as change, numbers, then evidence and limits

objectives: Assess your own competence against a trainer checklist
Complete the capstone evidence honestly

blocks.text: Certification in this course is not about attending; it is about evidence that you can design, deliver, evaluate and improve a training, and help others do the same. This lesson helps you check your evidence honestly and plan the next 90 days so your skills keep growing after the certificate.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.caption: Your certificate stands on the evidence in your portfolio.

blocks.text: Trainer self-assessment
Rate yourself on each competence from 1 (not yet) to 3 (confident), and note the evidence that supports your rating. Where you rate 1, plan one action in your 90-day plan.

blocks.text: Pass rule: you qualify for the certificate only after completing the practical capstone and scoring at least 70 percent in the final quiz. Submit only evidence that is real. If something is not done yet, finish it first.
Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: 90 days after certification
items: Days 1 to 30: deliver
Days 31 to 60: train trainers
Days 61 to 90: follow up
Day 90: report and review
blocks.caption: Deliver first, then multiply, then check that quality held.

blocks.title: Worked example: a realistic 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Blessing has completed the course and wants to cascade her savings group record keeping training through her church's women's fellowship in Port Harcourt.
steps: Days 1 to 30: deliver her training twice to 20 women each (40 in total), using her revised package. Record reaction and pre and post test data.
Days 31 to 60: select six trainers from those sessions using clear criteria, and run a two-day ToT with microteaching for each trainer.
Days 61 to 90: each trainer runs one session of about 15 women (target reach 90). Blessing observes three sessions with her checklist and calls the other three trainers after their sessions.
Day 75: she makes six-week follow-up calls to her first 40 participants to check behaviour.
Day 90: she writes a one-page report to the fellowship leader: reach, learning results, behaviour follow-up, observation scores and next steps.
blocks.result: Blessing's plan reaches about 130 women in 90 days, builds a team of six trainers, and keeps quality checks in place at every level.

blocks.title: Keep supporting your trainers
blocks.text: Create a WhatsApp group for your trainers to share questions, photos (with consent) and attendance lists. Hold a short check-in call every two weeks. New trainers are most likely to drift from the guide in their first few sessions, so that is when your support matters most.
Growing as a trainer

Trainers who keep improving tend to share three habits. They seek feedback after every session, not only when something goes wrong. They watch other trainers and borrow good techniques. And they keep evidence: logs, scores and reflections that show progress over time. Set yourself one improvement goal per month, for example "ask more open questions" or "finish every session on time", and review it in your trainer log.

As you start training other trainers, your role shifts towards that of a master trainer. You will spend more time designing materials, observing, coaching and checking quality, and less time delivering every session yourself. Plan for this in your 90-day plan by blocking out time for observation visits and check-in calls, not just for your own sessions.

Look after yourself as well. Training is tiring work, especially with travel, heat and long days. Build rest days into your plan, share the load with co-facilitators, and do not accept more sessions than you can deliver well. A trainer who is exhausted cannot give participants her best.

At day 90, compare what happened with what you planned: reach, test results, observation scores and follow-up findings. Note what you will keep, change or stop, and set your next 90-day goals from that review.

Keep learning too. Ask to co-facilitate with more experienced trainers, observe others, and keep your trainer log. Each training you deliver and evaluate makes your portfolio stronger and your cascade more reliable.

takeaways: Certification rests on real evidence, not attendance
Use the self-assessment to find gaps and plan actions
A 90-day plan: deliver, train trainers, follow up, report
Support new trainers closely in their first sessions
